correctness.rationale: Use the standard colour-refinement/C² equivalence in the adjacency-only language, comparing against arbitrary finite simple graphs. For n≤k+1 the vertex count and full degree force the complete graph. For k≥2 and t=n−k−1∈{1,2,3}, the degree formula min(i,k)+min(n−1−i,k) gives the distinct pairs A_i={i,n−1−i} with degrees k+i, plus a universal class (which is empty at n=6,k=2). Reflection makes each pair equitable and the universal vertices have identical quotient counts. Between distinct pairs i<j, same-side distances are ≤2≤k and opposite-side distance is k+t−i−j, so the block is complete for i+j≥t and a perfect matching otherwise. The matching subgraph on classes is a forest; its arbitrary matching choices can be normalized by flips propagated along each tree, leaving internal edges and complete blocks unchanged. This reconstructs any refinement-equivalent graph. For k=1, refinement peels distance-from-nearest-end classes, a chain of pair matchings with a central singleton if odd and a central within-pair edge if even. For k≥2,n≥k+5, A_0 and A_1 are distinct exact degree pairs; A_2 is also an exact degree pair when k≥3 and otherwise consists of the degree-four neighbours of A_0, distinguished by the next round. Reflection prevents any of these pairs from splitting. Their three interclass blocks are matchings, because opposite-side distances between distinct classes are at least n−4>k. The stated switch changes just the A_0–A_2 matching while preserving every stable-class neighbour count (and hence all round colours by induction). It reduces the count of triangles meeting all three intrinsic classes from two to zero regardless of within-class edges. Thus the switched graph is nonisomorphic and witnesses the claimed first obstruction, including n=7,k=2. The two finite Python checkers were inspected, not run; the proof covers the full quantifiers and does not rely on testing a comparison corpus.
